facts.F1: The appellant was established in 1857 in Italy as a manufacturer and vendor of headgear under the trade mark BORSALINO, the very rare surname of its founder.
facts.F2: BORSALINO acquired a world-wide reputation in the 1970s and early 1980s for clothing, perfumery, and leather goods.
facts.F3: The appellant's mark BORSALINO (in capital and script form) has been registered in Hong Kong in respect of clothing and perfumery.
facts.F4: The respondent, Wong Wai Sum, trading as Chi Hang Company, was not familiar with English and could pronounce English words by looking at their spelling.
facts.F5: Wong was not familiar with the mark BORSALINO when he invented the mark BORSALINI in discussions with his colleagues.
facts.F6: The respondent's colleagues assisted him with the correct spelling of the BORSALINI mark.
facts.F7: Wong did not know that BORSALINO was an Italian surname when he started selling leather wallets and handbags with the BORSALINI mark in the summer of 1983.
facts.F8: Wong's sales were primarily exports to Japan and Taiwan, only a small proportion being distributed to Hong Kong retailers (mainly leather goods speciality shops).
facts.F9: Leather goods marked BORSALINI accounted for some 70% of Wong's export sales.
facts.F10: There have been no complaints of confusion between the marks BORSALINO and BORSALINI.
facts.F11: Wong Wai Sum has since died and proceedings were carried on against his widow, Leung Hoi Yung, by an order of Liu J. on 19th October 1992.
facts.F12: The level of public inconvenience is a significant factor when determining whether to exercise discretion under section 22 of the Trade Marks Ordinance
facts.F13: The association of a trade mark with the goods of a 'fashion house' may create public inconvenience if a similar mark is registered in respect of similar goods
facts.F14: The BORSALINO mark has a broad reputation globally and in Hong Kong.

facts.F1: The Applicant submitted building plans to the Building Authority for approval for the redevelopment of Nos. 15 & 17 Sands Street, Hong Kong.
facts.F2: The plans proposed a 26-storey domestic building, but the Building Authority refused to give its approval on the ground that the carrying out of the works shown thereon would result in a building differing in height from the building previously existing on the same site.
facts.F3: The Building Authority's decision was contained in a letter dated 28th November 1991.
facts.F4: The Authority's main objection to the plans was that the density of development contemplated was excessive due to limited vehicular access to the site.

facts.F8: The Authority's decision was based on a policy decision promulgated in a circular in 1974, which stated that no buildings higher than existing buildings would be approved where access was limited.
facts.F9: Section 16(1)(g) of the Buildings Ordinance gave the Authority wide discretions to consider factors such as the safety of people in and around a building.
facts.F10: Each body, including the Building Authority, the Director of Fire Services and the Town Planning Board, had a different perspective and role in the process.

claim: Challenging the so-called 'blanket policy' of the Director not to permit mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants to work in Hong Kong, and seeking declaratory and other relief.
requested_remedy: Challenging the so-called 'blanket policy' of the Director not to permit mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants to work in Hong Kong, and seeking declaratory and other relief.
parties: Plaintiff: MA, GA, PA, FI, and JA

facts.F1: Five applicants, MA, GA, PA, FI, and JA, are mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants who have been stranded in Hong Kong for a prolonged period of time with little prospect of resettlement or departure in the immediately foreseeable future.
facts.F2: The applicants are not permitted to work in Hong Kong under the Director's immigration policy.
facts.F3: The applicants have made requests to the Director for permission to work, but their requests have been refused or are still pending.
facts.F4: The applicants argue that the Director's policy is irrational or unreasonable, and that it infringes their rights under various international instruments, including the Basic Law, the Hong Kong Bill of Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
facts.F5: The Director's policy is based on the need to protect the local workforce and maintain stringent immigration control.
facts.F6: The applicants have been provided with assistance and subsistence support by the Government and other agencies, but they argue that this is not sufficient to meet their needs.
facts.F7: The Director has a discretion to permit mandated refugees or screened-in torture claimants to work in exceptional circumstances.
facts.F8: The Director must take into account the individual circumstances of each applicant when exercising his discretion.

lawsuit_type: Judicial review

parties: Defendant: YKK AP HONG KONG LTD

facts.F1: The plaintiff and the defendant were engaged in eight building projects between 1998 and 2001, with around 30 contracts involved.
facts.F2: Disputes arose over payments, including retention money, variation works, and contra-charges.
facts.F3: The plaintiff left the site of the 8th and final project in 2001 and soon after went into voluntary liquidation.
facts.F4: The plaintiff claims it was owed $16 million by the defendant at the time, while the defendant claims it overpaid the plaintiff by $3,587,186.
facts.F5: The litigation has proceeded slowly since the writ was issued in August 2004.
facts.F6: The pleadings are complete, and the estimated trial length has increased from 11 to 20 days.
facts.F7: The defendant did not make an application for security for costs until December 2008, over four years after the writ was filed and six years after the plaintiff's liquidation.
facts.F8: The plaintiff incurred considerable costs without indication that an order for security would be made.

lawsuit_type: Security for costs application
